---
title: "Machine Learning Basics for Marine Science"
description: "A plain-English course for marine researchers who want to use machine learning well, and know when not to."
toc: false
---

Machine learning has become hard to avoid in marine science. It is used to map
habitats, identify species from images and sound, fill gaps in patchy time series,
and predict where animals will be next season. Much of it works. Some of it works
for the wrong reasons, and the difference is not always visible from the outside.

This course is for researchers who want to tell those apart.

## The intended reader

You work in marine science (ecology, oceanography, fisheries, genomics, acoustics)
and you know your own data and your own field well. You may have years of experience
with statistical models. What you have not had is a careful introduction to what
machine learning actually does, where it differs from the modelling you already know,
and which of its habits are dangerous in data like yours.

No prior machine-learning experience is assumed. Some familiarity with R helps, but
every example is written to be readable even if you would have written it differently.

## The shape of the course

Ten sections, meant to be read in order. Each explains an idea in plain English
first, then shows it working on marine data using
[tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org), then says plainly where it breaks down.

Marine data breaks several of the assumptions that machine learning quietly relies
on. Observations near each other in space or time are not independent. Sampling
follows ship tracks and good weather, not study design. The interesting class, a
rare species or a bleaching event, is usually the scarce one. These problems are not
footnotes here; they run through the whole course.

## The ten sections

| | Section | What it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Introduction](chapters/01-introduction/index.qmd) | What is machine learning, and how is it different from what I already do? |
| 2 | [Marine datasets](chapters/02-marine-data/index.qmd) | How do I get my data into a state a model can use, without cheating? |
| 3 | [Supervised learning](chapters/03-supervised-learning/index.qmd) | Which method fits my question: regression, classification, trees? |
| 4 | [How algorithms learn](chapters/04-how-algorithms-learn/index.qmd) | What is actually happening when a model "fits"? |
| 5 | [Generalisation](chapters/05-generalisation/index.qmd) | Why does a model that fits beautifully fail on new data? |
| 6 | [Assumptions & limitations](chapters/06-assumptions-limitations/index.qmd) | What is my model quietly assuming about the ocean? |
| 7 | [Validation](chapters/07-validation/index.qmd) | How do I know how good it really is? |
| 8 | [Unsupervised learning](chapters/08-unsupervised-learning/index.qmd) | What if I have no labels, only patterns? |
| 9 | [Neural networks](chapters/09-neural-networks/index.qmd) | What are they, and do I need one? (Usually not.) |
| 10 | [Interpretation & responsible use](chapters/10-interpretation/index.qmd) | What can I honestly claim from this model? |

## Work by participants

The [contributed pages](contributed/index.qmd) are analyses that course participants
built from their own data: real, messy, domain-specific problems rather than tidy
teaching examples. They are the most useful part of the site for seeing how the
methods survive contact with actual marine data.
